common_name: Fire Island Hosta (Chartreuse Hosta with Red Petioles)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fire Island develops its brightest gold leaf color and most vivid red petioles and stems with some morning sun, though it tolerates deeper shade with a more muted, greener leaf color.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving morning sun or bright dappled light for the best color contrast between foliage and stems. Fire Island is a compact, fast-growing hosta cultivar with smooth, chartreuse-to-gold leaves that turn a more vivid yellow-green as they mature through the season, set off dramatically by bright red-purple petioles and scapes that intensify in cooler weather and with more light exposure. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes above the foliage in mid to late summer. Its compact size and striking color combination make it an excellent edging or container hosta, and its vigorous, fast-multiplying habit means clumps fill in quickly compared to slower-growing hosta cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, and watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

common_name: Blue Ivory Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Creamy White Margin)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Ivory holds its blue-green leaf color best in deeper shade, since direct sun fades the waxy blue cast and can scorch the pale margins.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, avoiding direct afternoon sun, which fades the blue-green leaf color and can scorch the creamy margins. Blue Ivory is a medium-sized hosta cultivar with thick, heart-shaped, deeply veined blue-green leaves edged in a wide, irregular band of creamy white to ivory that brightens as the season progresses, creating strong two-tone contrast in a shaded border. Near-white flowers appear on scapes held above the foliage in summer. The heavy substance of its leaves makes it more slug-resistant than many thinner-leaved hosta cultivars, and its bold variegation reads well from a distance, making it a good choice for brightening a dark corner of the shade garden. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring as new growth emerges.

common_name: Curly Fries Hosta (Miniature Gold Hosta with Wavy Twisted Leaves)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Curly Fries develops its brightest gold color with a few hours of morning sun and holds up well as an edging plant or container specimen given its small mature size.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving a little morning sun for the brightest gold color on this novelty miniature. Curly Fries is a small, distinctive hosta cultivar with narrow, wavy, twisted gold leaves that curl and ripple along their length, giving the clump a texture unlike almost any other hosta and living up to its playful name. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer, but the foliage is the main attraction, forming a dense, low mound well suited to the front of a shaded border, a rock garden, or a container where its unusual form can be appreciated up close. Its small size makes it a good choice for gardeners with limited space who still want a distinctive gold hosta. Divide clumps every four to five years in spring if increased numbers are wanted, since the compact habit means division is rarely necessary for plant health.

common_name: Autumn Frost Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Gold Margin)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Autumn Frost keeps the strongest blue cast on its center in deeper shade, while the gold margin brightens with a little morning sun.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with some morning sun to bring out the brightest color contrast between the blue-green center and gold margin. Autumn Frost is a sport in the Frances Williams lineage of hostas, bearing thick, heavily corrugated, frosty blue-green leaves edged in a wide, irregular band of creamy gold that deepens as the season progresses, giving the clump a rich, layered color display from spring through fall. Near-white flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Its heavy leaf substance provides good resistance to slug damage compared to thinner-leaved hostas, and the bold, dual-tone foliage makes it an effective focal point or specimen in a shaded border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring as new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Rainforest Sunrise develops its brightest gold center with a few hours of morning sun, while the dark green margin holds its color well even in deeper shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun for the strongest gold color at the center of each leaf. Rainforest Sunrise is a sport in the popular Paul's Glory hosta lineage, bearing thick, cupped, corrugated leaves with a bright gold center bordered by a dark green margin, a striking reverse of the more common gold-margined pattern seen in many variegated hostas. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes held above the foliage in summer. The heavy leaf substance resists slug damage better than thin-leaved cultivars, and the bold gold-and-green coloring makes it a strong focal point in a shaded border or woodland garden. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring as new growth emerges.
